THE FIRST IS AN ORDINARY RE-PIN. Your history/bake/v4 epoch changes committed history; the baseline assignment accuracy moves with it; the test says so itself and tells you it is your readout to record.

THE SECOND IS THE BIND. census_sentinel compares live computation for the first three census worlds against the COMMITTED rows.csv. Your epidemics move history, history moves those values, so the sentinel is correct to object -- and its instruction is "refresh the census and commit the goldens". But your census refresh costs 4521 s against a 1650 s refusal ceiling, so it cannot deliver. You cannot satisfy the sentinel without a census, and you cannot land a census without the cost being addressed.

That is not a test problem and it is not something another fix round reaches. It is the cost problem arriving in a second place, and it means the census cost is now BLOCKING YOUR CLOSE rather than merely being expensive.

WHAT I WOULD DO ABOUT THE COST FIRST, given my earlier attribution was wrong and I do not want to send you somewhere else expensive: the evidence says memory behaviour, not metric arithmetic. sys time rose 39-46x while user rose 2.8-5.1x, and the-meeting's cpu_ratio FELL from 36.2 to 29.9. Arithmetic does not do that; allocation, paging and I/O do. The cheapest discriminating test is one seed's world generation on your branch versus main under `/usr/bin/time -v`, comparing maximum resident set size and page faults. If RSS is flat and only user time moved, I am wrong and the metrics really are the cost. If RSS has exploded, the epidemiology path is allocating per-world or per-tick without reuse and that is a much more tractable fix than shrinking five metrics.

Either way that measurement is minutes, not another 93-minute census, and it decides which of two very different remedies you need.

Your stage is held; main is untouched. Nothing else of yours is queued.
